Before you start

Students learn why the first months of college carry higher risk, why people don't step in, four ways to step in, and what to say if a friend tells them. Say at the start that some students may have experienced assault and anyone can step out, and never discuss what a victim should have done.

Every student in the room

On the talk-it-over questions, say plainly that assault happens to people of every gender, including men and transgender and nonbinary students, and in same-gender situations.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep your tone steady and warm. Then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

Say it slowly: some people in any room have experienced this, at home, at school, in a relationship. Not because of what you drank, wore, said or didn’t say. If you step out, I’ll check in after.

Slide 3 · Notes

Take a few guesses. The point: risk lives in new places with people you’ve just met, not dark alleys.

Slide 4 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 5 · Notes

Say plainly: men are often the least likely to tell anyone. Never discuss what a victim should have done.

Slide 6 · Notes

Most of the room stands; no stories needed. Responsibility spreads thin in a crowd, and a party is a crowd. Decide ahead of time that you’re the someone.

Slide 7 · Notes

Guys have extra pull: another guy saying “Not cool, man” often lands harder than anything else. Students with bystander training stepped in more (Coker et al., 2011).

Slide 8 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs. Quiet students often pick distract or delegate, and those count.

Slide 9 · Notes

Take four or five, then into the two nights.

Slide 10 · Notes

Everyone takes both nights, one at a time. Next slide shows one good move.

Slide 11 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 12 · Notes

Options: medical care within about five days, a confidential counselor or advocate, RAINN. Avoid any question that sounds like blame. Next slide shows one good move.

Slide 13 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 14 · Notes

Name the worries without pointing at anyone. Present options without assuming anyone’s family will or won’t be supportive.

Slide 15 · Notes

Rules vary by school: look them up. Reporting to police or Title IX is the survivor’s choice, and the evidence window for a medical exam is about five days.

Slide 16 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs. Nobody speaks for a group, and no personal stories.

Slide 17 · Notes

Take a few. Listen for strengths as well as costs.

Slide 18 · Notes

Share the student page link. Close with: “If anything today brought something up for you, come find me, today or any day.” Stay in the room a few minutes after.

If you want more

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students learn what the research says about sexual assault risk in the first months of college, why bystanders freeze and four ways to step in, and how to respond if a friend tells them something happened. The frame stays on bystander action and on the person who commits an assault.

Materials

  • Index cards, one per student
  • The student page link (last slide) to share afterward

Flow

  1. 2 minBefore we start: take care of yourself
  2. 4 minWho knew the person, and every gender
  3. 3 minWhy nobody steps in, and the four Ds
  4. 3 minWhich D fits you? Turn and talk, share out
  5. 5 minTwo nights: Nico at the party, the next morning
  6. 3 minWho’s confidential, and what to say first

Short on time (10-minute version)

Before we start (2), the four Ds (3), Nico at the party (3), what to say first (2).

Before you teach
Some students have experienced this.

Assume someone in the room has, at home, at school or in a relationship. Say so at the start, say it was not their fault, and say anyone can step out without explaining. Check in later with anyone who leaves.

Never ask what a victim should have done.

Questions about drinking, clothes or whose room it was put the blame on the wrong person. If a student goes there, use the icy sidewalk analogy: ice makes falls likelier, and the person who pushes you is always at fault.

No personal stories.

Keep every example invented. If a student starts to share their own experience, thank them gently, protect them from the room, and talk privately afterward.

Medical facts change by state.

Evidence collection usually needs to happen within about five days, and many states let you have an exam without reporting to police. Tell students to check the rules where they'll be.

RAs may not be confidential.

At many colleges, RAs must pass reports to the Title IX office. Counselors, health staff and advocates usually are confidential. Students should know who's who before they need it.

After the lesson.

If a student discloses, believe them, thank them, and follow up one on one that day. State your reporting limits up front, and don't promise secrecy you can't keep.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Every gender.

1 in 15 undergraduate men and 22.8% of transgender, genderqueer and nonbinary students reported nonconsensual sexual contact. Make sure examples include men and LGBTQ+ students as possible survivors, and say men are often the least likely to tell anyone.

Families, cultures and faiths talk about sex differently.

Some students grew up where sex and assault are never discussed. That can shape who a survivor tells. Present options without assuming anyone's family will or won't be supportive.

Calling for help isn't the same for everyone.

Some students fear police or immigration consequences. Name confidential advocates, campus safety and RAINN as options alongside 911.

Race and who gets believed.

Students of color and immigrant students may worry about not being believed or about how police will treat them or the person reported. Name that worry and the confidential options.

Disability.

Students with disabilities face higher risk and more barriers to reporting. Mention that advocates and disability services can help.

Not every student is going to a campus.

Students headed to work, the military or a gap year face the same risks in new places. The four Ds and the "if a friend tells you" steps work anywhere.

What the research says

Researchers call the stretch from move-in to Thanksgiving the red zone. In one campus study, first-year women were at higher risk of unwanted sex than second-year women, especially early in the fall. Other studies are more mixed on timing.

Kimble et al., 2008

At Division 1 schools, reports of rape involving victims aged 17 to 24 rose 28% on football game days.

Lindo, Siminski and Swensen, 2018

In a national study of college women, about 9 in 10 victims of rape or attempted rape knew the person who did it.

Fisher, Cullen and Turner, 2000

Since enrolling, 25.9% of undergraduate women, 22.8% of transgender, genderqueer and nonbinary students, and 6.8% of undergraduate men reported nonconsensual sexual contact by force or incapacitation. About 1 in 5 rapes and sexual assaults of female college students were reported to police.

AAU Campus Climate Survey, 2019 · Sinozich and Langton, Bureau of Justice Statistics, 2014

At least half of college sexual assaults involve alcohol, used by the person who commits the assault, the victim, or both. Someone who is incapacitated can't consent.

Abbey, 2002

People who believed they were the only one hearing someone have a seizure were much more likely to go for help than people who believed others could hear it too.

Darley and Latané, 1968

In a survey of about 2,500 undergraduates at one university, students who'd had Green Dot bystander training reported stepping in more and held fewer myths that blame victims.

Coker et al., 2011
